title: The 1-rupee water bottle: the full case study
summary: Market, customer psychology, the two-sided model, illustrative unit economics, competitors and a pilot plan for my GIM sustainability project: a ₹1 carton of water paid for by ads.

blocks.markdown:
*The full case study behind my GIM sustainability project. For the short version, read [the blog post](#case-one-rupee-water-bottle).*

The **1-rupee water bottle** is drinking water in a paper-based carton that sells for ₹1. Advertisers buy every face of the carton, and their money pays for the water, the bottling, the distribution and a margin. The cap carries a seed, so the last piece of the pack can be planted.

Here we look at the idea the way we would look at any company's: the market it enters, the customer behaviour it relies on, how the money flows, what one pack earns, who else is doing it, and what could break it.

items.title: The problem
items.text: Drinking water on the go comes in plastic, and India emits more plastic pollution than any other country.

items.title: The idea
items.text: A carton of water for ₹1, with ads on every face and a seed in the cap.

items.title: The tension
items.text: Ads could make it free, so why charge ₹1? Because a small price changes how people treat the pack.

blocks.heading: How to read the numbers
blocks.text: Market, waste and competitor figures come from the public sources linked beside them. Cost and volume figures for the pack itself are **illustrative**: they show how the model works, not what the project found.

blocks.markdown:
**Packaged drinking water** is water treated, sealed and sold in a container, from a 250 ml pouch to a 20-litre jar. In India it is a large, growing and crowded market.

1. **Size:** the market was worth about ₹32,040 crore (US$3.6 billion) in 2025 and is projected to reach ₹57,850 crore by 2032 ([IBEF, 30 March 2026](https://www.ibef.org/blogs/india-packaged-drinking-water-industry-demand-trends-and-market-outlook)). That works out to roughly 9% a year. e.g. the water bought at every railway platform, bus stand and wedding.
2. **A clear leader:** Bisleri earned ₹2,690 crore from operations in FY24 and spent ₹101 crore on advertising and promotion ([Goodreturns, on Bisleri FY24 filings, 8 January 2025](https://www.goodreturns.in/news/bisleri-fy24-profit-rises-82-8-percent-to-rs-317-crore-011-1398203.html)). It is reported to hold about 38% of the organised market ([Open, 16 February 2026](https://openthemagazine.com/branding-marketing-and-advertising/indias-15-vs-150-water-battle-can-premium-brands-justify-the-markup)). Hence a new brand cannot win on distribution or ad budget alone.
3. **Price-led competition:** large groups are entering at low price points, e.g. Reliance's Campa Sure at ₹15 ([Open, 16 February 2026](https://openthemagazine.com/branding-marketing-and-advertising/indias-15-vs-150-water-battle-can-premium-brands-justify-the-markup)). Thus price is already the main battleground, and ₹1 is a radical move within it.
4. **Most sales happen off the shelf:** over two-thirds of sales in 2024 were off-trade, through shops rather than restaurants ([IBEF, 30 March 2026](https://www.ibef.org/blogs/india-packaged-drinking-water-industry-demand-trends-and-market-outlook)). This means the kirana shop and the cart are where the ₹1 pack must win.

### The waste side

A 2024 study in *Nature* ranked India as the largest emitter of plastic pollution in the world, at about 9.3 million tonnes a year, roughly a fifth of the global total ([Down To Earth, on Cottom, Cook & Velis, Nature, 2024](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/waste/india-tops-plastic-pollution-rankings-emitting-a-fifth-of-global-plastic-waste)). Official CPCB figures put plastic waste generated in India at about 41 lakh tonnes in 2020-21 ([PIB, Ministry of Environment, 27 July 2023](https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1943210)).

Paper-based beverage cartons have their own record. A TERI study found 63.66% of used cartons recycled across 24 cities in 2025, which extrapolates to about 48% nationally, up from 29% in 2011 ([Tetra Pak India, on the TERI used beverage carton study, 26 November 2025](https://www.tetrapak.com/en-in/about-tetra-pak/news-and-events/newsarchive/aseptic-carton-recycling-rates-improving-teri-study)). India uses about 21 billion cartons a year, and that is expected to double by 2030 ([Waste & Recycling Middle East, 18 August 2026](https://www.wasterecyclingmag.com/news/sustainable-packaging/beverage-cartons-hit-48-recycling-rate-in-india-up-from-29-in-2011)). Hence a carton is not waste-free, but it enters a recycling system that is measured and improving.

blocks.heading: The strategic question
blocks.text: Can a water brand win by charging almost nothing, if someone other than the drinker pays for the pack, and can that same low price make people treat the pack better?

chapters.title: The customer: why ₹1 and not free

blocks.markdown:
**Price psychology** is the study of how prices change behaviour, beyond what they cost. For this idea, we need four effects.

1. **Zero-price effect:** free is treated as a different category, not a low price. When a 1-cent price cut made a Hershey's Kiss free, choice flipped from 73% Lindt to 69% Kiss ([Shampanier, Mazar & Ariely, Marketing Science, 2007](https://people.duke.edu/~dandan/webfiles/PapersPI/Zero%20as%20a%20Special%20Price.pdf)). e.g. we take free pens we do not need. Thus free maximises taking, not valuing.
2. **Screening:** a price, however small, filters for people who want the product. In Zambia, buyers who faced a higher price for a water purifier were more likely to use it ([Ashraf, Berry & Shapiro, American Economic Review, 2010 (J-PAL summary)](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/evaluation/can-higher-prices-stimulate-product-use-evidence-randomized-experiment-zambia)). e.g. a sachet bought at the kirana shop is bought for today. Hence the ₹1 pack reaches the thirsty, not the curious.
3. **Signalling:** a price tells people a thing has value. A coin changing hands turns a handout into a purchase. e.g. a pamphlet handed out at a signal is dropped in a minute, while a newspaper you paid for is read. This is the core claim of the project.
4. **IKEA effect:** we value what we put effort into. People who built IKEA boxes would pay about 63% more for them ([Norton, Mochon & Ariely, Journal of Consumer Psychology, 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IKEA_effect)). e.g. the seed in the cap invites a small effort, planting it, which gives the pack a reason to be kept.

blocks.heading: The counter-evidence
blocks.text: Two studies push back. The Zambia study found **no sunk-cost effect**: paying more did not on its own raise use ([Ashraf, Berry & Shapiro, American Economic Review, 2010 (J-PAL summary)](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/evaluation/can-higher-prices-stimulate-product-use-evidence-randomized-experiment-zambia)). In Kenya, free malaria nets were **not wasted more** than paid ones, while demand fell about 60 percentage points when the price went from zero to $0.60 ([Cohen & Dupas, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2010 (NBER)](https://www.nber.org/papers/w14406)). So the ₹1 is best defended as a filter and a signal, and the claim that it cuts littering is a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

chapters.title: The business model: two customers, one pack

blocks.markdown:
A **two-sided model** serves two groups at once, and one group pays for the other's access. e.g. a newspaper sells readers to advertisers, and the cover price is a small part of its income. The ₹1 carton works the same way: the drinker gets water, and the advertiser gets the drinker's attention.

Here we map it on the Business Model Canvas, keeping both customers in view.

blocks.title: Business Model Canvas
rows: Value proposition|Safe water for ₹1, in a carton, with a seed to plant|An ad held in the hand for several minutes, placed by location
Channels|Kirana shops, carts, stations, campuses, events|Direct sales team, agency partners
Relationship|Habit: the ₹1 pack becomes the default|Repeat campaigns, reports by location
Revenue|₹1 per pack|Price per pack carrying the ad
Key activities|Bottling, distribution, recycling tie-ups|Selling the space, printing, proving reach
Key partners|Bottlers, carton maker, seed supplier, recyclers|Brands, agencies, events

blocks.markdown:
### Why would a brand pay?

1. **Attention time:** a billboard gets a glance; a water pack is held while it is drunk. e.g. reading the label while waiting for a train.
2. **Placement:** the pack can be sent where a brand's buyers are, e.g. a gym brand on packs near gyms. Wahter geotags its carts for this reason ([afaqs!, 3 January 2024](https://www.afaqs.com/news/advertising/how-wahter-is-looking-to-make-water-bottles-an-advertising-medium)).
3. **A budget already exists:** Indian brands spent ₹4,140 crore on outdoor advertising in 2023, up 13% in a year ([Media4Growth, on the Pitch Madison Advertising Report 2024](https://www.media4growth.com/research/indian-ooh-adex-at-rs-4140cr-in-2023-records-13-yoy-growth-vs-10-overall-adex-growth-pitch-madison-ad-report-2024-7301)). Hence the pack does not need a new budget, only a slice of an existing one.
4. **A real price exists:** Wahter charges advertisers about ₹9–20 per bottle, depending on volume, location and minimum order ([afaqs!, 3 January 2024](https://www.afaqs.com/news/advertising/how-wahter-is-looking-to-make-water-bottles-an-advertising-medium); [YourStory, 6 March 2024](https://yourstory.com/2024/03/a-husband-wife-duo-leverage-tech-to-make-bottled-drinking-water-affordable)). This is the anchor for the unit economics below.

blocks.markdown:
**Break-even ad rate** is the ad revenue a pack needs so that it neither earns nor loses money. Here it is cost minus price: ₹8 − ₹1 = **₹7 per pack**. e.g. if advertisers pay less than ₹7, every extra pack sold loses money, however many we sell.

The table below shows the margin per pack as the two numbers we are least sure of change.

Two things stand out. First, the ₹1 price barely moves the result; the model lives or dies on **ad revenue per pack**. Second, at a pack cost of ₹10, even ₹9 an ad, the bottom of Wahter's range, only breaks even. Hence the first job in a real pilot is a firm carton quote and a signed advertiser rate.

Sources: Wahter ([afaqs!, 3 January 2024](https://www.afaqs.com/news/advertising/how-wahter-is-looking-to-make-water-bottles-an-advertising-medium); [Indian Startup News, 22 June 2024](https://indianstartupnews.com/funding/packaged-drinking-water-startup-wahter-raises-rs-5-crore-in-pre-seed-funding-4774808)), FreeWater ([The Daily Star, 17 January 2024](https://www.thedailystar.net/tech-startup/news/how-does-freewater-work-3522056)), Mizu ([The Business Standard, 17 January 2024](https://www.tbsnews.net/features/panorama/bottled-water-free-will-new-advertising-model-sustain-776254)), Campa Sure ([Open, 16 February 2026](https://openthemagazine.com/branding-marketing-and-advertising/indias-15-vs-150-water-battle-can-premium-brands-justify-the-markup)).

**What the comparison tells us:**

1. **The model has been proven in India:** Wahter claims 2 lakh bottles sold in its first month and raised ₹5 crore at a ₹52 crore valuation ([Indian Startup News, 22 June 2024](https://indianstartupnews.com/funding/packaged-drinking-water-startup-wahter-raises-rs-5-crore-in-pre-seed-funding-4774808)). Thus advertisers will pay for water packs here.
2. **The carton and the seed are the difference:** Wahter uses plastic. A carton with a seed cap competes on sustainability, which matters to brands that want a green message.
3. **Free has a retail problem:** in Dhaka, critics warned shopkeepers earn little on a free bottle and may not push it ([The Business Standard, 17 January 2024](https://www.tbsnews.net/features/panorama/bottled-water-free-will-new-advertising-model-sustain-776254)). Hence the ₹1 also buys the shopkeeper's interest.

chapters.title: Risks, and how a pilot would test them

blocks.title: Main risks
rows: Ad sales fall after launch|The whole margin is ad revenue|Sell 3–6 month packages; report reach by location
Carton costs more than a bottle|Raises the break-even ad rate|Get quotes early; start with one pack size
Cartons are not collected|Swaps one waste problem for another|Partner with carton recyclers; collection bins at sale points
Seed fails or cap does not break down|The sustainability story weakens|Test seed types for heat and storage; use a compostable cap
Shops will not stock it|No distribution, no reach for advertisers|Give a margin from the ₹1 and the ad income
Food safety and licensing|Packaged water needs certification|Bottle through certified partners

steps.text: Get carton, cap and filling quotes for 1 lakh packs. Fix the real break-even ad rate.
Sign two or three local brands before production. No ads sold, no pilot.
Sell at ₹1 in one area and give free in a matched area. Count sales, repeat buyers and packs found as litter.
Report reach to advertisers, ask for a second order, and decide whether ₹1 really beat free.

blocks.markdown: Location for the pilot: **[To confirm with Mathew]** (for example a college campus, a railway station or Goa's beaches).

1. **A small price is a design tool:** it filters customers, signals value and gives the retailer a reason to care. e.g. ₹1 does work that free cannot.
2. **In a two-sided model, find the real customer:** here the advertiser pays most of the bill, so the product must be designed for them too.
3. **Sustainability needs a business that pays for itself:** the slide said it best: *we sustain ourselves along with sustaining the world*. Hence the green idea only lasts if the margin is real.
4. **Test the claim you care about most:** the belief that paid packs are littered less is the heart of the idea, and also the least proven part. A pilot should measure it first.
